# Generating items {#aig}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain **automatic item generation** (AIG) from **item models**, and how
  it differs from asking a language model for items;
* write an item model with `item_model()`, with distractors built from
  misconceptions and constraints that rule out flawed items, and generate
  **isomorphs** with `generate_isomorphs()`;
* check after field testing whether a family of isomorphs is equally
  difficult with `calibrate_families()`, and find the variable that makes
  a family spread;
* fit a one-step model with a random item effect in mirt, or with eirm,
  and say when a family mean can stand in for a field test.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Item model](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-model),
[LLTM](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#lltm),
[calibration](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#calibration).

## The ideas

Testing programs need many items: For new forms each year, for adaptive
tests that must not expose the same items too often (Chapter
\@ref(banks-cat)), and for practice. Writing and field-testing each item by
hand is the slowest and most expensive part of test development.
**Automatic item generation** (AIG) writes items from a template
[@gierl2013; @gierllai2013]. An **item model** is a parent item with
variable parts: A stem, a key and distractors, each written as a template,
the values each variable can take, and constraints that every generated
item must meet. Filling in the values gives **isomorphs**: Items that test
the same thing in the same way and differ only in their surface, such as
the numbers.

Two promises come with item models. The first is quality at scale: If the
model is right, every item it generates is right, and an error in the model
shows up in every item, where an automatic check can catch it. The second
is **calibration at the level of the family**. If isomorphs are equally
difficult, the item model can be calibrated once, and its new items can use
the family's difficulty without a field test of their own
[@glas2003; @sinharay2003]. That promise is an empirical claim, and this
chapter is about checking it.

A family's items are never exactly equally difficult. The model for a
family $f$ is
$$b_i = \mu_f + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_f^2),$$
where $\mu_f$ is the family's mean difficulty and $\sigma_f$, the
**within-family SD**, says how much its isomorphs differ. A new item's
difficulty is predicted by $\mu_f$ with an error of about $\sigma_f$. When
$\sigma_f$ is small, the family mean is as good as a field test of a few
hundred test takers; when it is large, some variable in the item model
changes what the items demand, and the model must be split or the variable
added as a feature, as in the LLTM of Chapter \@ref(item-text). Explanatory
IRT treats this as one model with item features and a random item effect
[@deboeck2004; @geerlings2011].

Language models offer a second route: Ask for items in a prompt
(`generate_items()`, Chapter \@ref(llms)). They write more varied items,
but each is a one-off, with no template to calibrate and no guarantee that
two items with the same prompt are isomorphs. Template-based AIG is
predictable and traceable; every item can be rebuilt from its values. In
practice the two meet: Language models can help write item models, and
their items can be reviewed with the same checks.

## Example 1: Writing an item model

An average speed item has two variables, the speed `v` and the time `t`.
Writing the distance as `v * t` keeps the answer a whole number. Each
distractor is the answer of a misconception:

```{r data-aig-1}
# Item models for a simulated Grade 7 field test.
speed <- item_model(
  stem = "A train travels {v * t} km in {t} hours. What is its average speed?",
  key = "{v} km/h",
  distractors = c(multiplied = "{v * t * t} km/h", subtracted = "{v * t - t} km/h",
                  added = "{v * t + t} km/h"),
  values = list(v = seq(40, 120, 10), t = 2:6), name = "SPD")
frac <- item_model(
  stem = "A class of {n} students voted. {num}/{den} of them chose soccer. How many students chose soccer?",
  key = "{n * num / den}",
  distractors = c(multiplied_only = "{n * num}", rest = "{n - n * num / den}",
                  one_part_too_many = "{n / den * (num + 1)}"),
  values = list(n = c(12, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40), num = 1:3, den = 2:6),
  constraints = c("num < den", "n %% den == 0"), name = "FRA")
avg <- item_model(
  stem = "The heights of {k} plants are {paste(seq(a, by = s, length.out = k), collapse = ', ')} cm. What is their mean height?",
  key = "{a + s * (k - 1) / 2} cm",
  distractors = c(sum = "{k * a + s * k * (k - 1) / 2} cm", largest = "{a + s * (k - 1)} cm",
                  divided_by_wrong_n = "{(k * a + s * k * (k - 1) / 2) / (k - 1)} cm"),
  values = list(k = 3:5, a = c(10, 12, 14, 20), s = c(2, 4)),
  constraints = "(s * (k - 1)) %% 2 == 0", name = "AVG")
speed
```

Printing a model checks it: All 45 combinations of speed and time give
four different options. `generate_isomorphs()` draws items from the
combinations and puts the options in random order:

```{r}
x <- generate_isomorphs(speed, n = 3, seed = 15)
x$stem
as.data.frame(x[, c("id", "A", "B", "C", "D", "key")])
```

The fraction model is less safe. With $\frac{1}{2}$, the students who chose
soccer and those who did not are the same number, so the key and the `rest`
distractor are identical. `generate_isomorphs()` leaves such combinations
out, and says so:

```{r, message = TRUE}
fams <- generate_isomorphs(list(speed, frac, avg), n = 12, seed = 151)
table(fams$model)
```

Almost half of the fraction model's combinations were dropped, and two of
the mean model's. The message is a request to fix the model with a constraint, so that the next
person who uses it, or the software, does not depend on the check
(Exercise 1).

## Example 2: Calibrating the families

The 36 items were field-tested on 800 students. We simulate the responses:
Each family has its own difficulty, each item adds item-specific noise with
an SD of 0.2 logits, and fractions with a numerator above 1, which take
two steps, are 0.8 logits harder than unit fractions. Then we calibrate the
Rasch model.

```{r data-aig-2}
# Simulated field test of the generated items: 800 students.
set.seed(1515)
two_step <- !is.na(fams$num) & fams$num > 1
b_true <- c(SPD = -0.2, FRA = -0.4, AVG = 0.4)[fams$model] + 0.8 * two_step +
  rnorm(nrow(fams), 0, 0.2)
theta <- rnorm(800)
resp <- sapply(b_true, function(b) rbinom(800, 1, plogis(theta - b)))
colnames(resp) <- fams$id
rasch <- mirt(as.data.frame(resp), 1, "Rasch", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
pars <- tidy(rasch)
items <- as.data.frame(fams)
b <- pars[pars$term == "b", ]
items$b <- b$estimate[match(items$id, b$item)]
items$b_se <- b$std.error[match(items$id, b$item)]
```

`calibrate_families()` summarizes each family. Its observed SD includes
the estimation error of each $b$; with `se`, the error variance is
subtracted, which leaves the within-family SD. The 95% interval is where a
new isomorph's difficulty is expected to fall, and `field_n` translates the
prediction error into the size of a field test that would estimate the
item as precisely.

```{r}
cal <- calibrate_families(items, family = "model", se = "b_se")
cal
```

The speed and mean families are isomorphic, with within-family SDs of
about 0.2 and 0.3 logits: Their family means are worth a field test of
70 to 140 students. The fraction family spreads over almost two logits.
Sorting its items by difficulty shows why:

```{r}
fr <- items[items$model == "FRA", c("id", "num", "den", "b")]
fr[order(fr$b), ]
```

All five unit fractions are easier than all seven others. Splitting the
family by that variable gives four isomorphic families (Figure
\@ref(fig:aig-families)):

```{r}
items$family <- ifelse(items$model == "FRA",
                       ifelse(items$num == 1, "FRA-unit", "FRA-nonunit"), items$model)
cal2 <- calibrate_families(items, family = "family", se = "b_se")
cal2
```

```{r aig-families, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Item families after splitting the fraction model. Dots are items, diamonds family means, and bars the 95% interval for a new isomorph."}
autoplot(cal2)
```

The split is a substantive finding, not a statistical repair: Finding
$\frac{2}{3}$ of a number takes one step more than finding $\frac{1}{3}$
of it. The item writers can keep one model and treat `num > 1` as a
feature, or write two models; either way, the family mean of the original
model would have misled.

## Example 3: One step, with a random item effect

The two-step approach treats the estimated difficulties as data. A
one-step model fits the responses directly: The family is a fixed effect,
and each item's departure from its family mean is a random effect whose
variance is $\sigma^2$, pooled over families. mirt's `mixedmirt()` fits
it (the estimation takes about a minute):

```{r}
design <- data.frame(family = factor(items$family))
mm <- mixedmirt(as.data.frame(resp), model = 1, itemdesign = design,
                fixed = ~ 0 + family, random = ~ 1 | items, verbose = FALSE)
fixed <- summary(mm, verbose = FALSE)$fixed
data.frame(family = sub("family", "", rownames(fixed)),
           difficulty = -fixed[, "Estimate"])   # mirt models easiness; reverse the sign
sqrt(coef(mm)$items)                              # within-family SD
```

The family difficulties match the two-step means, and the within-family SD
is about 0.24 logits, close to the 0.2 that was simulated. This is the
LLTM of Chapter \@ref(item-text) with a random item effect, and the same
model fits as a generalized linear mixed model with the eirm package
[@bulut2021], from data in long format. Item features such as `num > 1`
can go into the same formula:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("eirm")
library(eirm)
long <- data.frame(person = rep(seq_len(nrow(resp)), ncol(resp)),
                   id = rep(colnames(resp), each = nrow(resp)),
                   resp = as.vector(resp))
long <- merge(long, items[, c("id", "model", "family")])
long$two_step <- as.integer(long$family == "FRA-nonunit")
m_eirm <- eirm("resp ~ -1 + model + two_step + (1|person) + (1|id)", data = long)
print(m_eirm, difficulty = TRUE)   # family difficulties and the two-step effect
lme4::VarCorr(m_eirm$model)       # person and within-family item variance
```

With the feature in the model, the original three item models stay, and
the fixed effect of `two_step` estimates how much the second step adds.
Hierarchical models of this kind can also give each family its own
variance and its own discrimination [@sinharay2003; @geerlings2011].

## Example 4: Does the family mean predict new items?

The real test of family calibration is a held-out one: Calibrate each
family on some of its items and predict the others as if they were new.

```{r}
number <- as.integer(sub(".*-", "", items$id))
old <- items[number <= 6, ]
new <- items[number > 6, ]
cal_old <- calibrate_families(old, family = "family", se = "b_se")
new$predicted <- cal_old$mean_b[match(new$family, cal_old$family)]
sqrt(mean((new$predicted - new$b)^2))
```

The family means miss the new items by about a quarter of a logit, about
what the within-family SDs promised, and three times the standard error of
an item calibrated on 800 students. That is precise enough to assemble
field-test or practice forms, and to start online calibration, where new
items are given as unscored pretest items and their own estimates replace
the family mean as responses come in. Whether it is precise enough for
scored items on a high-stakes test is a judgment about the decisions the
scores support, not a property of the data.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Add a constraint to `frac` so that no combination gives identical
   options, and print the model. Which fractions does your constraint rule
   out?
2. Without splitting the fraction family, fit
   `predict_difficulty(items, c("model", "num"), se = "b_se", methods = "lltm")`.
   What does the weight of `num` say, and how does its cross-validated
   error compare with that of the split families (`c("family")`)?
3. Widen the values of the speed model: Change `t` to `2:10` and `v` to
   `seq(5, 120, 5)`. Print the model. Are all items still flawless,
   and are they still isomorphs?
4. In Example 2, raise `max_sd` to 0.5. Which families now count as
   isomorphic, and what would that hide?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. a constraint for distinct options
frac2 <- item_model(
  stem = frac$stem, key = frac$key, distractors = frac$distractors, values = frac$values,
  constraints = c(frac$constraints,
                  "length(unique(c(n * num / den, n * num, n - n * num / den, n / den * (num + 1)))) == 4"),
  name = "FRA")
frac2
g <- expand.grid(num = 1:3, den = 2:6)
g <- g[g$num < g$den, ]
g$distinct <- with(g, num / den != 1 / 2 & den != 2 * num + 1)
g[!g$distinct, ]

# 2. the numerator as a feature
m_num <- predict_difficulty(items, c("model", "num"), se = "b_se", methods = "lltm")
tidy(m_num)
m_num$accuracy
predict_difficulty(items, "family", se = "b_se", methods = "lltm")$accuracy

# 3. wider values for the speed model
speed3 <- item_model(stem = speed$stem, key = speed$key, distractors = speed$distractors,
                     values = list(v = seq(5, 120, 5), t = 2:10), name = "SPD")
speed3

# 4. a looser threshold
calibrate_families(items, family = "model", se = "b_se", max_sd = 0.5)
```

1. The constraint that the four answers are all different leaves 31
   combinations. It rules out $\frac{1}{2}$ (also written
   $\frac{2}{4}$ and $\frac{3}{6}$), where the rest equals the key, and
   $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{2}{5}$, where the rest equals one part too
   many. Writing the general constraint is safer than listing the
   fractions, because it also holds after someone adds new values.
2. Each unit of the numerator adds about 0.4 logits, and the LLTM's
   cross-validated error (about 0.28 logits) is close to that of the split
   families (0.25): The feature does most of the work of the split. It
   does a little worse because the simulated effect is a step from unit to
   non-unit fractions, which a straight line in `num` only approximates.
3. All 216 combinations still give four different options, so the check
   passes. But a distance of 10 km in 2 hours and one of 1,200 km in 10
   hours are not the same task for a Grade 7 student: Larger numbers and
   less friendly divisions make items harder. Whether they are isomorphs is
   an empirical question that only a field test answers, and extending the
   values is a change to the item model that needs one.
4. With 0.5, the original fraction family (0.46) counts as isomorphic.
   Its interval for a new item then spans almost two logits: Every unit
   fraction item would be predicted about 0.45 logits too hard, and every
   other one about a third of a logit too easy.
   The threshold should come from how precise the family mean must be for
   its use, not be loosened to pass a family.

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Gierl and Haladyna [-@gierl2013] collect the theory and practice of AIG,
and Gierl and Lai [-@gierllai2013] give a short introduction to item
models. Glas and van der Linden [-@glas2003] and Sinharay, Johnson and
Williamson [-@sinharay2003] model item families with random item
parameters, and Geerlings, Glas and van der Linden [-@geerlings2011] add
the rules used to generate the items as explanatory variables. Bulut,
Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli [-@bulut2021] show how to fit such
explanatory models in R with eirm.
